The engineering problem

A robot becomes a system when its mechanical interfaces, electronics, and control conventions work together.

I led the mechanical and robotics development of a modular quadruped, working from SolidWorks assemblies to printed hardware and coordinated leg motion. A central design goal was making the joints and leg modules accessible for assembly, testing, and revision.

My contribution

  • Designed printed body and leg structures, actuator interfaces, and serviceable assemblies.
  • Developed analytical forward and inverse kinematics and checked the geometry against CAD.
  • Prototyped leg trajectories in Python and developed the Linux C++/Eigen control stack with SocketCAN.
  • Helped teammates work through assembly, CAN communication, and subsystem testing.

Geometry and analysis

Leg geometry needs a consistent joint convention before it can become a motor command. I used CAD measurements and handwritten derivations to connect joint angles with foot position, then compared analytical calculations in software.

Foot velocity and joint motion
vfoot = J(q) q̇

The Jacobian J relates joint rates q̇ to foot velocity at the current configuration q. Calibration, motor direction, gearing, and offsets are handled separately from the geometric model.

What the prototype demonstrated

PROJECT STATUS

Coordinated motion; reliable forward walking remains in development.

The assembled platform produced repeatable coordinated leg trajectories and limited backward, lateral, and crawl motion. I’m continuing work on calibration, single-leg behavior, and full locomotion. The robot’s operating electronics use off-the-shelf drivers; the custom controller-board project has its own development status.

The most useful lesson has been to isolate the problem. A coordinate sign, a mechanical clearance, and a communication timing issue can each look like a control failure until they are tested separately.
